title: Canopy Architecture, Light Interception and Microclimate Gradients

content.overview: A canopy is a three-dimensional light- and air-interception structure. Height, branch angle, leaf area, flower position and spacing create vertical and horizontal gradients that affect photosynthetic opportunity, humidity and product uniformity.

vocabulary.definition: Capture of incident photons by leaves and other plant surfaces within the canopy.
A change in a measured variable from canopy top toward lower layers.
Degree of open space that permits light and air movement through a plant canopy.

sections.title: Architecture changes exposure
sections.body: Cannabis architecture affects within-canopy light and microclimate. Upper tissues can intercept light before it reaches lower leaves and flowers.

sections.title: Uniformity requires spatial measurement
sections.body: Top-canopy averages can conceal shaded lower or edge zones. Measure light and environmental conditions at multiple heights and positions.

sections.title: Supplemental light can alter lower-canopy performance
sections.body: Recent interlighting research showed system-specific improvements in lower-canopy productivity/uniformity, but economics and thermal effects remain production-context dependent.

workedExamples: Two plants with the same height can create different lower-canopy light if one has denser lateral branching.
A high room-average PPFD does not prove inner flowers receive similar light.
commonMistakes: Treating plant height as a complete architecture metric.
Adding supplemental light before diagnosing the spatial deficit.
content.practicalApplication: Map PPFD and selected environmental measurements at top, mid and lower canopy while recording branch/flower positions and spacing.
content.summary: Canopy management begins with a spatial model of architecture, light and microclimate—not a single height or PPFD number.
